headline: Bacteria Treatment Saves Corals From Heat Wave in Red Sea
meta_description: Scientists in Saudi Arabia successfully used beneficial bacteria to prevent coral bleaching during a 2022 Red Sea heat wave, offering new hope for reef protect…
summary_short: A field study in the Red Sea proves that probiotic treatments can protect corals from bleaching during heat waves—a breakthrough from lab to real reef.
body:
When temperatures spiked in the Red Sea in 2022, a patch of corals 15 kilometers off Saudi Arabia's coast stayed vibrant while nearby reefs faded. The difference: these corals had been treated with probiotics—beneficial bacteria isolated from healthy corals themselves. The treatment prevented bleaching, according to research published in September by scientists at King Abdullah University of Science and Technology (KAUST). Even more promising, a heat-killed version of one bacterial treatment worked equally well, potentially offering a cheaper, shelf-stable alternative to live probiotics. For the first time, researchers had proven that such interventions could work not in laboratory tanks, but in the wild, during actual heat stress.

Corals are in crisis. They provide habitat for roughly one-third of marine species, yet they're declining at an unprecedented rate. Rising temperatures cause bleaching—a breakdown of the relationship between corals and the algae living inside them—that can lead to death. Scientists warn that if global temperatures rise 1.5°C above pre-industrial levels, 70 to 90 percent of corals face severe degradation by 2100. Principal investigator Raquel Peixoto had previously shown probiotics worked in tanks, but field success was crucial. During the 2022 heat wave, when Red Sea water temperatures reached 32°C (about 2°F above local summer average), her team dove eight times over 15 days to administer bacterial treatments to corals. Those treated maintained their color and photosynthetic efficiency, while untreated corals declined.

Challenges remain before wide deployment becomes possible. The researchers treated only one coral species and acknowledge that others will likely need their own bacterial cocktails. Yet the results suggest nature itself offers the toolkit—if we can learn to use it. "Corals can acclimate and adapt, but only if they are alive," Peixoto said. For reefs facing relentless warming, that survival matters more than ever.
quick_facts: Red Sea study treated corals 15 km off Saudi Arabia coast during 2022 heat wave
Probiotic bacteria isolated from healthy local coral species prevented bleaching
Heat-killed version of treatment also worked, offering cheaper alternative
Water temperatures reached 32°C, about 1.2°C above summer average
First field proof that probiotics protect corals in wild, not just labs
